chapter_theme: The second half of the rains: the man, his work done, tells his charioteer and his heart that the flowering woodland calls him home (21, 22, 24, 28-33, 36), while the friend alternately shows the waiting wife the season as proof he will come and lets her own distress, or his broken word, show (23, 25-27, 34, 35, 37-40).

21.reading: The returning man tells his charioteer that all along the road the well-made, sturdy chariot has come, the small mullai buds stand in their prime, pointed like the sharp teeth in the mouth of the simple girl of fragrant brow, rich, cool wide eyes and few words.
21.nuance: The usual simile runs from woman to flower (teeth like jasmine buds); here it runs from flower to woman, so every bud on the road home already shows him her mouth.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai buds in their prime along the road home

comparisons.tenor: the small mullai buds, white and pointed

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்); the colophon names the speaker தலைமகள், but the verse is the returning man's (see source_issues)

22.reading: The returning man says that with the young attendants making merry in the cool wet land and the plumed, grass-fed horses yoked, the woodland has bloomed, lovely as the young beauty of good women and rich as the prosperity of the wealthy.
22.nuance: The two similes hold both ends of his journey in one forest: the beauty of the woman he is going back to and the wealth of those who prosper, the thing such journeys were made for.

thinai_evidence.note: the woodland in flower in the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்); the colophon names the speaker தலைமகள், but the verse is the returning man's (see source_issues)

23.reading: The friend says that the cloud has poured out so that cool drops and hailstones, like round shapely pearls, roll over all the woodland, and the sky has gathered its beauty: why then, girl of bright bangles, keep to your sulking?
23.nuance: The friend treats the sulk as out of date: the season he named has arrived, so the grievance has lost its ground. The same closing line ends verse 38, where the colophon gives it the opposite force.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain and hail over the woodland fix the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: the cool drops and hailstones rolling over the woodland

24.reading: The man tells his heart to rise and go, leaving all the work lying, for the woman whose thick dark hair smells like the musth of the bull elephant in the rocky forest cannot bear it any longer, and the rain-cloud is beginning, gently, to show its rain.
24.nuance: எல்லா வினையுங் கிடப்ப, 'let all the work lie', sits oddly with the colophon's வினைமுற்றிய (his work done): either the rest of the business is left to wait, or the rain has overtaken him before the task is finished.

thinai_evidence.note: the first gentle rain of the dark season

comparisons.tenor: her thick dark hair and its fragrance

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names the speaker தலைமகள், but the verse is the returning man speaking to his own heart (see source_issues)

25.reading: The friend, letting her own distress show, says that in the cool wet woodland the therukhi has opened its buds like puffed grains of black-stemmed millet, and at the thought that the signs he set have all come while he has not, the pallor has thickened on her friend.
25.nuance: The friend speaks of the heroine in the third person (அவட்கு) and voices the worst herself, so that the heroine, hearing it, is left to be the one who bears up; the same half-line returns in verse 40 as the thought the sky cures.

colophon.thurai: பருவங்கண்டழிந்த தலைமகள் ஆற்றல்வேண்டித் தோழி தனது ஆற்றாமை தோன்ற வுரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the woodland flowering in the season he named

26.reading: The friend says that the thondri has blossomed over every field, lovely as the first-night lamps the people set out in the auspicious month of Karthigai, and the rain has come bearing a message of few words.
26.nuance: The rain is made a messenger (தூது) of few words: he has sent no word of his own, so the season speaks for him; the variant மென்மொழி would make the message soft rather than brief.

thinai_evidence.note: the thondri in flower over the fields in the rains

comparisons.tenor: the red thondri flowers over the fields

27.reading: The friend says the sky roars and rumbles like the music of Murugan's rite and the woodland has bloomed with kurukilai; if we sulk, dwelling on the parting and saying he left without a thought for us, pallor will spread over her in her bed.
27.nuance: The friend says யாம், 'we', taking a share in the sulk in order to talk her out of it: a quarrel needs the man present, and turned on an absent man it feeds only the pallor. The rite of Murugan is hill-country (kurinji) music heard in the mullai thunder.

colophon.thurai: ஊடுதலாற் பசலைமிகும் எனத் தோழி தலைமகட்குக் கூற வற்புறுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the thunder and the flowering woodland of the rains

28.reading: The man tells his heart that with the sky booming and thundering and the kumizh flowers hanging in clusters like ear-pendants wrought of gold, the road through the cool ripe season is at its best for going to his beloved's town and quieting its gossip.
28.nuance: கவ்வை is the talk his absence has stirred in her town; his return is meant to end the talk as well as her grief, so the gossip that belongs to secret love follows the married pair into separation.

thinai_evidence.note: the thunder and the cool season of the rains

comparisons.tenor: the hanging clusters of kumizh flowers

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names the speaker தலைமகள், but the verse is the returning man speaking to his own heart (see source_issues)

29.reading: The man tells his heart that the groves nearby have blossomed, the fine bees hum without rest like bards singing in the woodland, and the clouds, foes to the parted, have come from every quarter: let us go, for the road is at its best.
29.nuance: The bees sing a bard's song, so the woodland performs the welcome a returning man's bards would; பகை, 'hostile', makes the cloud an enemy of those apart, whose arrival is a summons home.

thinai_evidence.note: the flowering groves and humming woodland of the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names the speaker தலைமகள், but the verse is the returning man speaking to his own heart (see source_issues)

30.reading: The man tells his heart that with the hills brimming, the sky at its height and sweet rain hanging low and breaking into drops over the wide earth, the cool fragrant grove, stirred by a wind that spreads its scent, speaks to us of the great innocence of our simple girl.
30.nuance: The grove's scent recalls her, and the poem makes the grove the speaker: what reaches him is not her message but the land telling him of her.

thinai_evidence.note: the brimming hills and the sweet rain

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names the speaker தலைமகள், but the verse is the returning man speaking to his own heart (see source_issues)

31.reading: The man tells his charioteer that the season when the handsome bull-buffalo, going down to the water by the banks the rains have flooded far, struts with the creepers it has tossed on its horns like warriors proud in battle, is the sign he set for the woman of the fair brow.
31.nuance: The warriors of the simile are the man's own company: the buffalo comes up from the flood like soldiers home from war, as he is; the buffalo of the watered fields is a marutham thing on a mullai road.

thinai_evidence.note: the banks flooded far by the rains

comparisons.tenor: the bull-buffalo strutting with creepers on its horns

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்); the colophon names the speaker தலைமகள், but the verse is the returning man's (see source_issues)

32.reading: The man tells his charioteer to drive on, now that the rains are running, through the woodland where bees, glad as the hearts of wealthy men who crave undying fame, hum like bards on the pidavam: it is good for the noble one.
32.nuance: A puram ideal, the rich man's pleasure in being sung for his gifts, is used to measure a bee's joy, so the woodland on the road home becomes a patron's court full of singers.

thinai_evidence.note: the woodland in the running rains

comparisons.tenor: the bees' gladness as they hum

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்); the colophon names the speaker தலைமகள், but the verse is the returning man's (see source_issues)

33.reading: The man tells his charioteer that, to end the grief of his simple, soft-spoken girl, he fixed as his sign the time when the cloud, heavy as with young after drawing up the sea, would be taken into the breast of the western mountain.
33.nuance: The promise is dated by the sky, not the calendar: the full cloud reaching the western hill is the appointed day, so the season itself becomes his word.

thinai_evidence.note: the full rain-cloud drawn from the sea

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்); the colophon names the speaker தலைமகள், but the verse is the returning man's (see source_issues)

34.reading: The friend, letting her own distress show, says that he named, for the bright-browed woman adorned with beauty, the season when the mighty sky, having drunk its fill of the wide-waved sea, gathers dark on the great hills.
34.nuance: She states only the fact, that this is the season he named, and leaves unsaid that he has not come; that silence is the distress the colophon says she lets show.

colophon.thurai: பருவங் கண்டழிந்த தலைமகள் ஆற்றல்வேண்டித் தோழி தனது ஆற்றாமை தோன்ற வுரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the dark-clouded season he named

35.reading: The friend says that as her friend, thinking that their beloved who went has passed far beyond, grows heavy with grief joined to pain, the lovely sky rumbles like a victorious war-drum and stays there rumbling, as if in pity for her.
35.nuance: இரங்கும் is both 'rumbles' and 'grieves for': the thunder that ought to announce his return sounds instead like pity for her, and the drum of victory recalls the war that keeps him.

colophon.thurai: பருவங் கண்டழிந்த தலைமகள் ஆற்றல்வேண்டித் தோழி தனது ஆற்றாமை தோன்ற வுரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the thundering sky of the rains

36.reading: The returning man tells his charioteer that the cool thalavam buds, lovely as kingfishers' beaks, have opened in rows, and the town of the simple girl with rich, cool, proud eyes and few words will be a good feast for us.
36.nuance: விருந்து makes the husband a guest at his own home: after the long absence he will come to her town as to a feast. Line 3 repeats the epithets of verse 21.

thinai_evidence.note: the thalavam, a mullai flower, opening in the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்); the colophon names the speaker தலைமகள் (வினைமுற்றி மீளுந் தலைமகள்), but the verse is the returning man's (see source_issues)

37.reading: The friend asks whether, even in this season of great rains, when the cloud heavy as with young that grazed on the black sea climbs the great rocks of the steep hills, our man who took up the king's hard task will fail to come.
37.nuance: வாரார்கொல் is reassurance put as a question. The king's hard task explains his absence and also vouches for him: a man fit for the king's work is one who keeps to an appointed time.

thinai_evidence.note: the season of great rains

comparisons.tenor: the cloud drawing up the sea

38.reading: The friend says that even in this cool season, when the fierce, tall bull elephant with its spotted face rolls in the dust and plays in accord with his mate, he has not come: why then, girl of bright bangles, this sulking?
38.nuance: The closing line is verse 23's, but here, by the colophon, the friend concedes that he has broken his word and the question about sulking asks what good it does.

colophon.thurai: தலைவர் பொய்த்தாரெனக் கூறித் தோழி தலைவியை ஆற்றுவித்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the cool season of the rains

iraicchi.act: the bull elephant plays in accord with his mate when the cool rains come
iraicchi.sense: even the elephant keeps company with its mate in this season, so the man who stays away has broken his word and the grievance is just

39.reading: The friend says that now the men wearing the green leaves of the dark-clustered nochchi, whose buds have opened like crabs' eyes, have begun ploughing the wide dry fields, he has become the great talk of our town.
39.nuance: கௌவை, the town's talk, is turned on him rather than on her: it is he who has become the byword for a broken promise. The crab is a shore creature borrowed as an image for a mullai bush.

colophon.thurai: தலைவர் பொய்த்தாரெனக் கூறித் தோழி தலைவியை ஆற்றுவித்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the ploughing of the dry fields that the rains allow

comparisons.tenor: the opened buds of the nochchi

40.reading: The friend says that for the woman who grieved that the signs he set had come but he had not, the lovely sky has taken on the dark colour of the indu and become the medicine to end her sickness: the brow of my simple girl will regain its brightness.
40.nuance: The sky does not bring him; it is itself the cure, because its dark colour proves the season and so his return. The first line repeats verse 25's despairing thought word for word, now as the thing the sky answers.

colophon.thurai: பருவம் வந்தமையால் தலைவர் வருதல் ஒருதலையெனக் கூறித் தோழி தலைமகளை ஆற்றுவித்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the darkened rain-sky

links.note: Kuruntokai 240: the waiting woman sees mullai buds like a wild cat's teeth (வெருக்குப்பல் லுருவின் முல்லை) crowding the bush as the north wind comes and his hill sinks at evening. Kar Narpathu 21: the returning man sees the mullai buds pointed like the teeth of his girl.
links.teaches: The same bud-and-teeth simile becomes a predator's teeth for the waiting woman and the beloved's teeth for the returning man, so the mullai bud's meaning in these poems is set by which side of the separation is looking, not by the flower.

links.note: Both close with the same line, ஒண்டொடி யூடுநிலை. In 23 the friend shows the season to reassure; in 38, by the colophon, she concedes that he has lied.
links.teaches: One closing question about sulking serves first to dismiss the heroine's grievance (the season has come, so he will) and then to grant it (the season has come and he has not), so the series uses a formula line whose force is fixed only by the lines before it.

links.note: Akananuru 47: if we have finished the work here, rise quickly, heart (வினைஇவண் முடித்தனம் ஆயின்). Kar Narpathu 24: rise, heart, leaving all the work lying (எல்லா வினையுங் கிடப்ப). On a plain reading they disagree on whether the task must be done before he turns home.
links.teaches: The older poem holds the man's return behind the finishing of his task, while the venba's man drops the task once the rain and the memory of her hair reach him, so the same address to the heart sets duty and love in two different orders.

links.note: Both see the thonri open like a lamp in the rains: in Akananuru 235 (சுடர்கொள் அகலின்) the heroine asks whether he has forgotten them; in Kar Narpathu 26 (கார்த்திகை ... விளக்கிற்) the friend says the rain has come with his message.
links.teaches: The lamp-like thonri is evidence that he has forgotten for the heroine and evidence that he has sent word for the friend, so the one sign of the promised season can be read against him or for him depending on who speaks.

links.note: Kural 1187: she turned aside a little from his embrace and the pallor was on her thick enough to scoop up. Kar Narpathu 27: if we sulk that he left without a thought for us, pallor spreads over her in bed (பள்ளியுட் பாயும் பசப்பு).
links.teaches: The couplet's hyperbole, that the least turning away from him in bed brings pallor, becomes in the friend's mouth a practical warning against sulking at an absent man, so the venba shows the Kural's figure used as an argument for bearing up.

links.note: Kural 231: to give and live so that renown arises; there is no other gain for a life. Kar Narpathu 32: bees glad as the hearts of wealthy men who crave undying fame (கெடாஅப் புகழ்வேட்கைச் செல்வர் மனம்போற்).
links.teaches: The couplet states the craving for renown through giving as the one gain of life, and the venba treats that craving as so familiar that a returning lover can measure a bee's gladness by it, which shows the puram ideal already turned into common stock for akam imagery.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 447: may the king's work be released, and then we shall see her bright brow, when the bee opens the red thalavu bud shaped like a kingfisher's beak (சிரல்வாய்ச் செம்முகை). Kar Narpathu 36: the man returning from the work sees the thalavam buds, lovely as kingfishers' beaks (சிரல்வாய் வனப்பின), opened in rows.
links.teaches: The same thalavu bud is the hour hoped for in the man's prayer while the king's work holds him and the sight on the road once he is released, so read together the bud marks the two ends of a single wait.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 37: will our man, who took up the king's hard work, not come even in the season of great rains? Akananuru 304: in the king's war camp as the first rains fall, the man fears she will think him unkind, not knowing his pain.
links.teaches: The friend's confidence rests on the season alone, and the Akananuru shows that season from inside the king's camp, where the man is still held and can only dread her reproach, so the king's work she counts to his credit is the very thing keeping him away.

links.note: Akananuru 85: the friend says the cool rains, when the elephant feeds his young mate and calf with bamboo shoots, are the season he promised, so do not weep. Kar Narpathu 38: the bull elephant plays with his mate in the cool season, yet he has not come, and the colophon says the friend tells her he lied.
links.teaches: The elephant pair in the rains is the friend's proof of his promise in one poem and her proof of his breach in the other, so the creatures' act carries the same sense in both while the verdict on the man turns on whether he has come.

links.note: Natrinai 267: crabs of the sand dune with eyes like the nochchi's dark buds (நொச்சி மா அரும்பு அன்ன கண்ண). Kar Narpathu 39: nochchi buds opened like crabs' eyes (அலவன்க ணேய்ப்ப).
links.teaches: The simile runs in opposite directions: the neythal poem makes its shore crab the subject and borrows the nochchi as image, while the mullai venba makes its nochchi the subject and borrows the crab, so each poet takes the tenor from the poem's own land.

links.note: Both turn on the same words, செய்குறி வாரா ரவரென்று: in 25 the friend says that thought thickened the heroine's pallor; in 40 she says the darkening sky has become the medicine for the woman who grieved at it.
links.teaches: The series states one despairing thought twice, once as the cause of pallor in the friend's confession of her own distress and once as the sickness the sky now cures, so her speeches of despair and of comfort rest on the same premise and differ only in how they read the sky.

source_issues: 21, 22, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33 (and 24, 36): the colophons read வினைமுற்றிய தலைமகள் (36: வினைமுற்றி மீளுந் தலைமகள்), but each verse is the returning man speaking to his charioteer or his heart; தலைமகன் is meant.
21 line 3: மழைந்தடங்கட் reads as a misprint for மழைத்தடங்கட், cool wide eyes (compare 36 line 3, மழைமதர்க்கட்).
24 line 3: பணிநோனாள் is taken as பனி நோனாள் (cannot bear the cold); the sense is unsure and the verse is marked uncertain. Line 1 கிடப்ப sits uneasily with the colophon's வினைமுற்றிய.
29 line 4: கரம் reads as a misprint for சுரம், the road (compare 28 line 3, சுரநெஞ்சே); பகைகொண்டல் is split across lines 2 and 3.
30: the verse ends on the participle உரைத்து and its construction is incomplete; marked uncertain.
32 line 4: பிடாஅப் பெருந்தகை நற்கு is hard to construe (whether பெருந்தகை is the man or the woman is unclear); marked uncertain.
33 line 2: பிறைக்கும் is not clear (the variant gives பிறக்கும்); marked uncertain.
37 line 2: இயுர்க்கும் is not a known form; the sense 'pours' is taken from context.
39 line 3: மேர்க்கடி is read as ஏர்க்கடி, the start of ploughing; the line's sense is uncertain.
40 line 3: இந்தின் (of the indu) is a rare plant name; the variant களிவண்ணம் changes the colour word.
